Comments:
I worked as a field service technician, but the questions relating to what field of IT I was in were hard to correctly answer.
Also, I am retired, so there are questions that don't take that into consideration.

Having older or more experienced staff on a team is critical to success in my opinion. Wisdom at a young age is very rare, and it is far too common that the management of teams isn’t familiar with the technology or problems faced by their staff. That said, dedication to continued education is critical for workers to remain relevant in this field. Although the core foundations and principles haven’t changed in my lifetime, the concepts and complexities of technology and platforms look very different from decade to decade, and not remaining current can make you irrelevant quickly.
My company is very large and has a large contingent of older workers, most of them have been working there 20+ years

As a reasonably young person (age 28), I actually find the reverse is true for me. Many of the most difficult and entitled people I’ve worked with (who also seem to do the least amount of work), are middle aged people (not very old). It’s interesting to me - do they feel a sense of completion when they hit 40 and believe the ‘younger crowd’ should do the dirty work? This my personal subjective experience obviously, but 9 times out of 10, if I’m working with a person aged 35-55, I know I’ll have a terrible shift. Whereas younger coworkers are a lot more fair in the distribution of tasks and no hierarchy seems to exist within younger generations (in my experience).

Generally old age people are not that bad. The problem is how their personal circumstances shaped them and how content they feel doing the job and embracing the workplace as a friendly environment. Both professional learning, openness and personal circumstances matter.

My responses related to discrimination more relate to when I was younger.  I've also had a family member forcibly early retired from tech at 60 though they were still at the top of their field.

I feel that age discrimination has changed over the last 20 years, but that there is still a stigma for those over 55 and those younger than 25.  The middle is typically left alone.

Experience can be discriminated as a proxy for age: Many times I have had to shorten my resume (only include the last 1-2 jobs) to get callbacks. Feedback I have received from my full resume was that I was "too experienced for a senior level position". This is likely indirect ageism.

I don't like this question because if I answer I Agree, it seems like I want to segment off older folks. I think there should be sports clubs of various levels so that folks can participate at their level of ability and competence. It is very helpful to all ages to do sports. Sometimes folks that are young will not be able to compete at a higher level.

Things should be based on skills and abilities.
In my opinion, Many old people did not plan very well for retirement especially health care insurance and expenses.

I'm not a misanthrope - I love being around humans - but we are what we are.

Comments: Regarding how "I feel" I have been treated at the workplace. I felt much less appreciated and trusted when I was in my 20's. As I got older, that changed dramatically. These questions were an interesting insight for me and my views towards ageism.

I feel the is a natural separation of people due to age, similar to cultural separation. The age gap exists and people react to it differently. The thing that I found often attributed to age (I may have done this in the past, but hope not) is the lack of contemporary training of older employees is seen to be a lack of competency rather than education. I came into the workforce in the age of the web. We have since moved through data growth and streaming. Younger co-workers are very knowledgeable about these topics and assume they are baseline types of knowledge needed. In some cases this is true, but the world is bigger that the focus of the immediate change and younger workers can miss this. I have also found order job canidates who may be very competent,  but are unfamiliar with the modern game of technical interviewing, thus they are not prepared to discuss specific algorithms, and are only prepared to discuss accomplishments. Ageism clearly exists, but I don't not always see it as prejudice, but a natural separation of life experience and narrow concerns about immediate goals of the workplace.
